To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cancer cells have a normal mitochondrial respiration and that the O(2)-consumption rate is governed by the availability of O(2) in cancer cells.

the mitochondria of cancer cells usually function as normal and that the oxygen consumption rate of cancer is determined by the availability of oxygen, which is the major factor limiting tumor growth.
the mitochondria of cancer cells are functional, and that the oxygen consumption rate of cancer tissue is determined by oxygen availability, not by the mitochondrial function of cancer cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) Is mitochondrial dysfunction a common feature in cancer cells?
the following questions: What are the metabolic changes that occur during malignant transformation and how are they linked to the malignant phenotype of cancer cells?
the following questions: What is the role of the mitochondrion in tumor cell metabolism?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mitochondrial respiration of most cancer cells functions normally and that the Warburg effect, as defined in the 1950s, is not valid.
the Warburg effect is not a consequence of mitochondrial dysfunction but of a reprogrammed cancer cell metabolism.
mitochondrial respiration is not impaired in the majority of cancer cells and that O(2)-limited metabolism is the major determinant for the O(2)-consumption rate of solid tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although the Warburg hypothesis is not valid in the original sense, the concept that cancer cells have a high demand for energy and biosynthetic precursors is valid.
the O(2)-dependence of tumor growth is a function of tumor size, i.e., the larger the tumor the more O(2)-deprived its cells become.
the Warburg effect, as originally conceived, is an artifact of the experimental conditions used to study cancer cells in vitro and that the in vivo situation is different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic phenotype of cancer cells is not a consequence of a dysfunctional mitochondrial metabolism.
cancer cells are not fundamentally different from their normal counterparts with regard to their energy metabolism and that they do not require a special energy supply to grow and divide.
the O(2)-consuming capacity of cancer cells is normal.
